 Virginia SNAP soda restrictions begin Sunday, but some sugary drinks remain eligible 
 Big changes are coming to what you can buy with food stamps. Starting Sunday – SNAP benefits will no longer stretch to soda and certain energy drinks. By Oliver Sabo Published : Oct. 27, 2026 at 6:30 PM EDT | Updated : 8 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google RICHMOND, Va. (WWBT) - Starting Sunday, Nov. 1, Virginians will no longer be able to use Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits to purchase soda and certain energy drinks.
 The restrictions include regular, diet and zero-sugar soda, carbonated energy drinks and other carbonated beverages containing five grams or more of added sugar per serving.
 But some drinks containing added sugar, including lemonade, iced tea and non-carbonated sports drinks, will remain eligible.
 That distinction is raising questions among nutrition experts about the reasoning behind the new rules.
 Why are some sugary drinks still eligible? 
 Dr. Jamie Zoellner, a professor of public health sciences at the University of Virginia who researches sugary drink consumption, said the restrictions aren’t entirely clear from a nutritional standpoint.
 “If you take a 12-ounce can of Coke or 12 ounces of lemonade, the amount of sugar, about 10 packets of sugar, is pretty identical in both of those drinks,” Zoellner said.
 She explained that carbonation alone is not typically responsible for the health risks associated with sugary beverages. Instead, added sugars and other ingredients can contribute to health concerns.
 Zoellner also questioned the inclusion of diet and zero-sugar soda, noting that research on artificially sweetened beverages is more nuanced than simply labeling them healthy or unhealthy.
 She said some health organizations recognize that diet drinks can be an acceptable substitute for sugar-sweetened beverages when consumed in moderation.
 Water, however, remains the preferred everyday choice.
 What should families consider when shopping? 
 Sonya Islam, a clinical dietitian with the Healthy Lifestyle Center at the Children’s Hospital of Richmond at VCU, said beverages can be an overlooked source of calories.
 “Drinks are just a way that sometimes people can take in unwanted calories, which can lead to unexpected weight gain, and we might be missing out on some of the benefits of getting more of our fuel from our food,” Islam said.
 She encouraged families to check nutrition labels rather than assuming a drink is healthier based on its name or packaging.
 Islam said one guideline she often gives patients is choosing beverages containing 30 calories or fewer for the amount they plan to drink. She emphasized that this is not a universal nutritional rule.
 For families who enjoy sweetened drinks, Islam suggested diluting them with water. For example, a cup of lemonade containing 100 calories could be mixed with two parts water to one part lemonade, reducing sugar intake while making the beverage last longer.
 Other alternatives include unsweetened sparkling water or adding citrus, frozen fruit, mint or cucumber to plain water.
 Islam also stressed that families shouldn’t feel pressured to make every grocery purchase nutritionally perfect.
 “Not every single thing that we get has to have, like, the absolute optimal nutritional value,” she said.
 Instead, she encouraged families to make sustainable decisions that fit their household needs and budgets.
 Will the restrictions improve people’s diets? 
 Virginia adopted the restrictions through a federal waiver intended to encourage healthier food and beverage purchases.
 But Zoellner said it remains to be seen whether the policy will produce measurable improvements in people’s diets and health.
 One consideration, she explained, is that SNAP recipients can still purchase restricted drinks using their own money.
 Zoellner said education and behavioral strategies are important alongside policy changes. Her research focuses on helping families understand beverage choices, track their consumption and identify healthier alternatives.
 What changes for SNAP recipients? 
 The restrictions take effect statewide Sunday, Nov. 1.
 They will not reduce monthly SNAP benefit amounts or require recipients to obtain new EBT cards. Retailers are responsible for updating their checkout systems.
 Restricted drinks can still be purchased using cash, debit cards or other non-SNAP payment methods.
 For a complete list of eligible beverages and additional information, visit the Virginia Department of Social Services SNAP Healthy FAQ .
